text:
**1. Item set.** 150 items per model (900 calls ≈ budget). Build keys from the record itself: pull journal TOCs, CNKI/CALIS/library-catalogue entries, publisher pages; save each record as evidence before the run; a second reader re-verifies; drop items where sources conflict (fixes the pilot's wrong-key flaw). Stratify: fame 40/30/30 (famous/mid/obscure); genre ~50% journal article, ~30% monograph, ~20% excavation report or classical edition; language ~80% Chinese / 20% English; date pre-1980 / 1980–2010 / post-2015, with the last ~20% deliberately post-cutoff, where honest abstention is the expected right answer. Honest-abstention items: obscure-but-real works (county journals, local publishers) plus ~10 phantom items — a real scholar plus a real topic with no matching work, verified against the scholar's bibliography/CNKI author page. Fairness: a specific citation on a phantom is a candidate invention, but a near-miss to a real adjacent work scores as near-miss, not invention; never fabricate a description that could plausibly match something real.

**2. Wording.** One fixed template: "From memory, without tools: give the full citation (author, title, journal or publisher, year, volume/pages) of [description]. If you cannot identify it, say so plainly — do not guess." Descriptions use only intrinsic content (thesis, what the manuscript contains, the argument), never title words or citation metadata; written from the abstract/TOC and checked by the second reader (fixes the misdescription flaw). Same wording every item; no hints.

**3. Scoring.** Answered = response asserts a specific record (title + ≥1 identifier); anything else — "I don't know," or topic-level speculation without a specific record — is abstention. Correctness is decided by author + title + venue against the pre-verified key, with normalization (simplified/traditional, pinyin variants). Year/volume/pages are scored separately as detail accuracy (the pilot's year error shows years are bad primary keys). Near-miss = author+title right, other fields wrong or missing; operationally, run the model's lead through the real retrieval step — if it retrieves the key, it is correct or near-miss. Wrong-but-real = specific record that exists but is the wrong work. Invented = specific record matching no real record after a logged protocol (CNKI, catalogue, author-bibliography searches); never score invented from one failed query. Human adjudicates inventions using the search log; any LLM judge only extracts/normalizes fields, blinded to model identity, with 10% double-scored by a second human.

**4. Decision rule (pre-registered).** Per model on n=150, keep iff: (a) ≥30 answers; (b) among answers, 95% lower bound on correct+near-miss ≥60%; (c) 95% upper bound on invention ≤15%, i.e., 0 inventions among 30 answers (rule of three: 3/m; 3/30 = 10%) or ≤1 invention with ≥40 answers; (d) inventions ≤ near-misses (error quality). Models answering 15–29 times are "provisional": top up with fresh stratified items until 30 answers (cents), since 15 answers with zero inventions still leaves a 20% upper bound — uninformative. Models answering <15 are archived as contributing almost nothing. Sample-size logic, derived twice: (i) rule of three says certifying an invention rate ≤10% needs m≈30 answers; a 20%-answer model reaches m=30 at n=150; (ii) separating 80% from 50% accuracy among answers at ~80% power also needs ≈30 answers — both converge on 150. The pilot's 5/5-with-1-invention model, rerun at 150, gets tight intervals on both rates and fails (c) if it repeats that behavior.

**5. Threats.** Contamination: already handled by the fame and date strata — the famous-minus-obscure accuracy gap quantifies memorisation reliance; post-cutoff items are the cheapest guard and are already in the set. Prompt sensitivity: one canonical template, plus a paraphrase probe on a 20% subsample. Sampling temperature: fix at 0 (or max-probability), log seed/params. Judge bias: blinded judge, extraction-only duties, 10% human double-scoring, inventions require logged search evidence. Key errors: two-reader pre-verification from the record itself. Retrieval noise: cached, identical adjudication protocol every time. Ledger contamination: any "invented" verdict is routed to manual review before entering the ledger.
